title: Sign Shop Letter Blocks
story: A sign shop builds lettering from pre-cut wooden blocks: single letters, plus blocks for common groups like th, ing and bake, since one block mounts faster than four. The workbench rule is that, reading left to right, you always take the longest block that fits the next letters exactly, or a single letter if none does.

Some language-model tokenizers use the same longest-match-first rule to cut text into pieces from a fixed vocabulary. That is why a common word is often one token while a rare word breaks into several.
task: Write tokenize(text, pieces). Start at the first letter. At each position, find the longest string in pieces that appears in text starting exactly there. Add it to the result and move past it. If no piece matches, add the single letter at that position and move one step.
Return the list of tokens in order. Joined together they must spell text. An empty text gives an empty list.
constraints: text and pieces use lowercase letters a to z only. pieces may contain repeats.

examples.explanation: At position 0 both "ba" and "bake" fit, and the longer one, "bake", is taken. At position 4 the piece "ry" fits, while "er" does not start there. The result is ["bake", "ry"].

At position 0 the piece "th" fits. At position 2 both "in" and "ink" fit, and the longer one, "ink", is taken. At position 5 the piece "ing" fits. The result is ["th", "ink", "ing"]. The greedy rule does not look ahead, so it never considers "in" followed by "king", even though that split would also cover the text.
No piece starts with "z", so it becomes a single-letter token. Then "oo" fits, so the result is ["z", "oo"].

hints: In the first example, "ba" and "bake" both fit at position 0. If you took the first piece in the given order that fits, which would you pick?

The rule asks for the longest match, so the order of pieces must not matter. You could check every piece at every position and keep the longest. How many checks is that for a long text and a big vocabulary?

Reverse the question. Instead of asking every piece whether it fits at this position, look at the text and ask whether the next 4-letter chunk is a piece, then the next 3-letter chunk, then the next 2-letter chunk. A set answers each of these in one step.

Put the pieces in a set and note the longest piece length L. At position i, try lengths from min(L, remaining) down to 2 and take the first substring that is in the set. If none is, take one letter. Then advance i by the length taken.
bruteForce: At every position, check every piece and keep the longest that starts there. With 10,000 letters and 1,000 pieces of up to 20 letters, that is up to 200 million character comparisons.
Only about 20 lengths are possible at any position, and a set says whether a chunk is a piece in roughly one step, so you can check those few lengths instead of checking every piece.

js: * @param {string} text  the letters to cut up
py: def tokenize(text: str, pieces: list[str]) -> list[str]:

tests.note: piece longer than what is left
defeats searching anywhere instead of at the position

js: for (const p of pieces) longest = Math.max(longest, p.length);
// Try the longest possible piece first, then shorter ones.
len = Math.max(len, 1); // a single letter is always allowed
py: longest = max((len(p) for p in pieces), default=1)
# Try the longest possible piece first, then shorter ones.
while length > 1 and text[i:i + length] not in vocab:
length = max(length, 1)  # a single letter is always allowed
walkthrough: The greedy rule never undoes a choice, so the only question is how to find the longest fitting piece quickly.
Trace "bakery" with pieces ["ba", "bake", "ry", "er", "y"]. The longest piece has 4 letters, so L = 4.
• At i = 0, try "bake" (4 letters). It is in the set, so the token is "bake" and i becomes 4.
• At i = 4 only 2 letters are left, so try "ry". It is in the set, so the token is "ry" and i becomes 6.
• At i = 6 the text is finished, and the result is ["bake", "ry"].

Greedy matching is fast and predictable, but it does not always give the fewest tokens. With pieces ab, abc and cd, the text "abcd" becomes "abc" and "d" instead of "ab" and "cd". Real tokenizers accept that trade-off. A trie would avoid re-reading letters, but with short pieces the set is simpler.
solution.timeWhy: At each of up to n positions you try up to L lengths, and building or hashing each substring costs up to L.
solution.spaceWhy: The set of V pieces, plus the output tokens.
solution.takeaway: For greedy longest-match, try the longest candidate length first at each position and take the first one that is in the set. Many tokenizers split text this way, and the same approach fits any dictionary-based segmentation that wants the biggest piece that fits.
